items.passage: What do you say to someone who left without a word and comes back the same way? I asked myself that at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I had gone to meet Zofia, our cousin, eleven years after she boarded a coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes; I had not. Our shop sold fewer radios each month, and he talked about it on the drive as if Zofia might bring customers in her suitcase. She stepped down carrying one small bag and kissed us both, and she explained nothing. I waited for an apology that never came and was surprised to find I did not need it. Watching her laugh at Marcus's terrible jokes, I thought the years had cost her more than they had cost us. A cleaner moved between the empty bays, pushing a wide broom over oil stains shaped like countries.

options: Forgiving, and inclined to imagine what Zofia has endured
Resentful, and determined to hear Zofia explain her absence

items.passage:
Anacleto,
I am writing from the projection booth, where the old machine still smells of oil and dust even though no film has run through it since spring. Your father's plane arrived this morning, wrapped in a flour sack, with a note saying he wished me to have it. I know you expected it. You swept his shop for six years before I ever held a chisel, and I have seen you run your thumb along that blade as if greeting someone. I will use it, because refusing a dead man's gift seems worse than accepting it badly. But every board I smooth will be a board I owe you, and I mean to keep the account. Tell your mother the booth's door finally closes; I rehung it on Tuesday with new hinges.
Cleotilde

Uneasy, since she regards the gift as a debt owed to Anacleto

items.passage: Three rules for lessons, Grandfather Kerem says: no English, no dictionary, no laughing at his handwriting. Tonight we broke all three in the boarding-house kitchen while the kettle muttered on the stove. I had found the letter last week inside his old grammar book, addressed to a woman named only by an initial, and I asked him to teach me enough to read it myself. He agreed too quickly. Tonight he made me copy one sentence about the sea eleven times, and when I finally read it aloud, he turned toward the window and said my vowels were still too round. I think he is glad someone will understand it at last, and afraid of exactly the same thing. A neighbor's cat slept on the bread bin again; tomorrow I must buy more sugar.

Embarrassed at having read a private letter without asking

items.passage: Once, in a cabin buried to its windowsills in Tromso snow, a young cook named Emil received a gift from his stern uncle Silas: a pair of fine leather gloves, two sizes too small. Emil thanked him warmly and wore them to stir the porridge, though his knuckles pressed white against the seams. For a week he praised their softness, and for a week Silas watched him fumble the ladle. On the eighth morning, Silas set a second pair beside the stove, wide and plain and lined with wool, and said nothing at all. Emil put them on and, for the first time all week, laughed. In the old telling, the two of them then shoveled a path to the woodpile while the northern sky went green above the drifts.

Amused by Silas's stubborn refusal to admit his mistake

items.passage: Beside the counter of the little post office outside Porto Alegre, Dalia weighed the parcel twice before paying. Inside was the manuscript of her new novel, bound for Matheus, who had translated her last three books. Years ago he had borrowed her grandmother's fountain pen to sign a contract and had never returned it; she had mentioned it once, lightly, and then not again. Lately his letters arrived signed in that same green ink, and she found she no longer minded. The pen had gone on writing her sentences in another language, which seemed to her a kind of return. The clerk, a young man with ink on his cuffs, stamped the parcel and tossed it into a canvas sack already bulging with seed catalogs.

items.passage: Was there a polite way to sit beside someone who had just mispronounced the name of your school in front of forty parents? I took the seat by the window anyway, and Kalani took the aisle, and the night bus pulled away from the hall in a hiss of brakes. For the first ten minutes she studied her phone, and I studied the dark shops of Chengdu sliding past. Then she asked me, very quietly, to say the name again so she could practice. I said it. She repeated it, wrong, and then nearly right. I had planned to stay angry until at least the weekend, but my resolve was fading faster than I liked. At the next stop, a vendor climbed on with a basket of steamed buns and walked the aisle calling out prices.

items.passage: "Same as always?" Shamsuddin asked, and Danish nodded, which was most of their conversation for the afternoon. Every Thursday for forty years, the two men had come back to the music room of the Karachi school where they had once been students, to tune its tired harmonium and dust the tabla skins. Neither was paid. Neither, as far as I ever saw, suggested stopping. As a boy I sat on the bench and watched them work, my grandfather pressing keys while his friend adjusted reeds, and I thought them dull. Only later did I notice how each corrected note seemed to answer the one before, like a sentence the other could finish. When Danish died, Shamsuddin came the next Thursday alone and tuned the instrument to the same pitch. Afterward the room was locked, and the key hung on a nail in the headmaster's office.

items.passage:
Dear Fumiko,
I lost again. You will be pleased, though you will pretend otherwise when we meet at the club. I am writing from a train compartment somewhere in Hokkaido, with our travel set balanced on my knees, replaying the endgame you won on Sunday. For twelve years we have played every week, and for twelve years neither of us has mentioned the tournament in Osaka or the move you swear you did not take back. I used to think our silence was cowardice. Lately I suspect it is the only reason we still sit across from each other. The snow here has buried the fences entirely; only the tops of the telegraph poles mark the road.
Yours in rivalry,
Rukhsana

items.passage: Years ago, on the promenade by the Lagos sea, a nephew named Casey owed his uncle Babatunde the price of a fishing boat. Each evening Casey walked the seawall with coins in his pocket, meaning to pay, and each evening he bought roasted corn instead and told himself tomorrow. Babatunde saw this from his bench and said nothing. When at last Casey came with the full amount, the old man counted it twice, then pressed half of it back into his hand. "The other half paid for the waiting," he said, "and I would buy that again." Casey walked home with the coins heavy in his fist, unable to meet the eyes of the corn seller. The tellers say she still keeps her fire burning on that promenade until the last ferry docks.

items.passage: Paper remembers every fold. Sharda had told her daughter this a hundred times in the bookbinder's workshop in Dhaka, usually while correcting a crease Samira had made too quickly. Now Samira's suitcase stood by the door, and her bus left for the university at noon. Last month they had quarreled over the scholarship letter Sharda had hidden for two weeks, afraid of an empty house. Samira had not forgiven her, and the apology Sharda finally offered had arrived, like the letter, too late. This morning Sharda stitched a blank notebook by hand, choosing the heavy cotton thread she usually saved for paying customers, and slipped it into the suitcase without a word. Afterward she swept the trimmings from the floor and lit the small lamp above the press.

items.passage: I had kept the lamps and gates of our old metro station in Seville for nineteen years when the surveyor arrived from Madrid. Everyone said Esteban had come to recommend closing the platform, and I believed it, so I polished every rail and swept the stairs twice before dawn. He spent the morning measuring tiles and asking which trains ran late. His questions were the kind I asked myself on sleepless nights, not the kind a man asks when his mind is made up. At noon he asked to see the flood marks on the eastern wall, the ones I had painted over years ago at my supervisor's request. I hesitated, then scraped the paint away with my key. He photographed each line carefully. That evening a busker set up by the turnstiles and played the same three songs until the last train.

CHULSOO: It was in the sun.

CHULSOO: (quietly) On stage, you mean.
GIULIETTA: I mean the sugar.

GIULIETTA: (not looking at her) Second act. Every night. A little to the left of my light.

items.passage: When I married Reid, I inherited a mother-in-law who had cooked in a ship's galley out of Kingston for twenty years and believed every meal should fit in one pot. My family set tables with seven small dishes, each in its own bowl. The first Sunday we cooked together in that narrow galley, docked for the holiday, she watched me arrange my bowls along the steel counter and said nothing. The next Sunday she brought a tray I had never seen, divided into compartments around a deep center, and set her stew in the middle. I learned later she had bought it across the harbor and carried it home on the bus in the rain. She never mentioned it. Reid still eats from the center first and works outward, which his mother calls bad manners.

### lit40-medium-01-005 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude

What do you say to someone who left without a word and comes back the same way? I asked myself that at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I had gone to meet Zofia, our cousin, eleven years after she boarded a coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes; I had not. Our shop sold fewer radios each month, and he talked about it on the drive as if Zofia might bring customers in her suitcase. She stepped down carrying one small bag and kissed us both, and she explained nothing. I waited for an apology that never came and was surprised to find I did not need it. Watching her laugh at Marcus's terrible jokes, I thought the years had cost her more than they had cost us. A cleaner moved between the empty bays, pushing a wide broom over oil stains shaped like countries.

[질문] Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Zofia?
A) Forgiving, and inclined to imagine what Zofia has endured
B) Resentful, and determined to hear Zofia explain her absence
C) Hopeful, and eager for Zofia to rescue the struggling shop
D) Indifferent, since the narrator barely remembers Zofia at all

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
화자는 사과를 기다렸지만 그것이 필요하지 않다는 사실에 놀랐다고 말하고, 웃는 Zofia를 보며 세월이 자신들보다 그녀에게 더 큰 대가를 치르게 했다고 생각한다. 두 단서는 원망 대신 용서하며 그녀의 고생을 헤아리는 태도를 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 설명을 끝까지 요구하지 않으므로 틀리고, C의 가게를 살려 줄 것이라는 기대는 Marcus의 태도이며, D는 화자가 Zofia를 무심하게 대하지 않으므로 맞지 않다.

For a week he praised their softness, and for a week Silas watched him fumble the ladle. On the eighth morning, Silas set a second pair beside the stove, wide and plain and lined with wool, and said nothing at all. Emil put them on and, for the first time all week, laughed.
